issues.issue: The Property is described only as "approximately 10.89 acres" with the actual legal description left to Exhibit 1, so the boundaries of what is optioned are not fixed on the face of the grant.
Section 5 requires an updated survey combining the vacated Sixth and Abbott Streets into a single parcel, so the parcel granted here may differ from the Exhibit 1 description.
This sentence makes the Option assignable only "to Optionee's developer," while Section 13 says the Option "may be assigned by the Optionee, without the consent of the Optionor" with no such limit.
"Shall continue in effect for a period of not less than one (1) year" sets a floor but no outside date, so "its expiration" has no ascertainable meaning and the Option's duration is genuinely open.
A fixed thirty-day extension is hard to reconcile with Section 2's open-ended "not less than one (1) year" term, since there is no fixed date from which the extension runs.

The stated "total purchase price" of $9,000,000 is only partly payable in money: the remaining balance is payable under the same Section 3 solely out of TIF reimbursements the Developer may never receive.
"Standard deductions and prorations," parenthetically explained as "customary closing expenses," gives no ascertainable measure of what may be added to or subtracted from the $8,000,000.

The clause makes the balance payable "at a rate of 10% of the annual tax incremental financing reimbursement received by Developer" without saying who owes the payment or what happens if no reimbursement is ever received.

Section 4 requires conveyance "upon payment of the Purchase Price, less the Outstanding Balance," leaving unclear whether this deferred payment is a debt of the Optionee or of the non-party Developer.

The Outstanding Balance is defined inside an illustration introduced by "For example," so whether the $1,000,000 figure and $200,000 annual payment are binding terms or mere illustration is genuinely open.
Interest accrues "to the same extent, if any," that a third party pays interest to the Developer on "outstanding incurred eligible expenses," a measure that may never be ascertainable.
Awarding the tax incremental reimbursement to the Developer sits awkwardly with the payment mechanism earlier in Section 3, which diverts 10% of that same reimbursement to Optionor.

This defines "Permitted Exceptions" as the items set forth in Exhibit 1, while Section 6 defines the same term as those title conditions not objected to or accepted by Optionee; the two definitions can diverge.
A survey to be delivered thirty days after the Effective Date is said to be already "attached hereto" as Exhibit 2, which the attachment list describes as "Survey & ALTA Survey Instructions."
The trailing phrase "by December 31, 2006" can attach either to Optionor's duty to provide the updated survey or to the Optionee's desired street closures, changing what is due when.

The promise of a policy "without standard exceptions" and "free and clear of any liens and encumbrances" cannot easily be squared with Sections 4 and 6, which contemplate conveyance subject to Permitted Exceptions.
The sentence imposes the duty on "Seller" in favour of "Purchaser," terms this Option never defines, leaving the obligor uncertain on the face of the clause.

The clause offers a choice "of either" and then lists three alternatives, and option (3) ends by giving Optionor, not Optionee, the discretion to substitute a surety bond, muddying whose election it is.
This definition of "Permitted Exceptions" (conditions not objected to or accepted by Optionee) conflicts with Section 4, which defines Permitted Exceptions as those items "set forth in Exhibit 1."
The representation mixes an unqualified statement (possession "has been peaceable and undisturbed") with knowledge-qualified ones, so how far the knowledge qualifier reaches is uncertain.
Utilities are warranted to be of "sufficient size, capacity" and available "for its current use" — a benchmark tied to current use, not the 266,200 sq ft federal facility the parties contemplate.
"All environmental information that it has" is undefined in scope and time, and it is unclear whether it is a continuing duty or a snapshot representation.
The representations are bring-down only "until and including any exercise of this Option," although Section 9 places Closing up to 90 days after exercise and Section 4 requires conveyance then.
"Reasonably cooperate" to determine the "most cost effective and appropriate" Due Care activities sets no standard by which either party's performance can be measured.
"Best efforts to obtain the maximum allowable reimbursable costs" is undefined and unbenchmarked, so what discharges the duty is genuinely open.
The defined term "Limitation of Liability" is attached to a $500,000 cap on one narrow item (unapproved Due Care costs), leaving it arguable that it caps Optionor's liability generally.
Section 12 also deducts amounts "up to the Limitation of Liability" for unapproved Eligible Activity costs, and nothing says whether the two deductions share a single $500,000 cap.

The deduction is taken from the Outstanding Balance, but under Section 3 that balance is payable only out of TIF receipts and under Section 12 may be retained by Optionee, so the remedy may be illusory.
This contemplates exercise "by Optionee or its Developer," while Section 2 gives the power of exercise to the Optionee by notice and Section 13 governs assignment.

An "as is" conveyance sits against Section 7's environmental and utility representations and Section 8's allocation of Due Care costs to Optionor, and the carve-out "except as otherwise provided" does not say which controls.

"Any other due diligence matters deemed reasonably prudent" is a catch-all appended to a specific list (test borings, plans, surveys, environmental assessments), and its reach beyond those kinds of activity is uncertain.
"Reasonable notice" is undefined, and unlike Section 20 it prescribes no form or period, so its content must be supplied by construction.

The approvals are introduced by "may include, but not be limited to" followed by seven specifics, leaving the reach of the open-ended category — and thus the scope of the parties' acknowledged obligations — uncertain.

The preceding paragraph lists many required approvals (Brownfield Plan, utility relocation, rezoning, site plan, special use permit), but Optionor is made responsible only for street vacations and zoning variances, leaving the rest unallocated.
"As soon as practical" fixes no time and the clause names no mechanism or decision-maker for determining whether land must be acquired.
Termination runs from "a final determination of those costs," but the Option never says who makes that determination or when it becomes final.
